title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: A photon of energy $7$ eV is incident on a metal surface having a work function of $3 \cdot 75$ eV. The stopping potential is :
questions.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation gives the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons :

$$K_{\max} = hf - \phi_0 = 7\ 	ext{eV} - 3 \cdot 75\ 	ext{eV} = 3 \cdot 25\ 	ext{eV}.$$

The stopping potential $V_0$ is the retarding voltage that just halts the fastest electron, so

$$eV_0 = K_{\max} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_0 = 3 \cdot 25\ 	ext{V}.$$

Working in electron-volts is what makes this a one-line subtraction: because $K_{\max}$ comes out in eV, the stopping potential in volts is the same number.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Light of frequency $6 \cdot 4 \times 10^{14}$ Hz is incident on a metal of work function $2 \cdot 14$ eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV, correct to two decimal places. (Take $h = 6 \cdot 626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s.)
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — energy of the incident photon.**

$$E = hf = \left(6 \cdot 626 	imes 10^{-34}ight)\left(6 \cdot 4 	imes 10^{14}ight) = 4 \cdot 241 	imes 10^{-19}\ 	ext{J}.$$

**Step 2 — convert to electron-volts**, dividing by $e = 1 \cdot 602 	imes 10^{-19}$ C :

$$E =  rac{4 \cdot 241 	imes 10^{-19}}{1 \cdot 602 	imes 10^{-19}} = 2 \cdot 65\ 	ext{eV}.$$

**Step 3 — subtract the work function.**

$$K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 2 \cdot 65 - 2 \cdot 14 = \mathbf{0 \cdot 51\ 	ext{eV}}.$$

The photon energy only just exceeds the work function, so the electrons come off slowly — the usual situation near the threshold frequency.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Photoelectric emission does not occur at all below the threshold frequency, no matter how intense the light. This shows that:
questions.solution:
A wave theory says a dim light should eventually deliver enough energy if you wait. It does not — **emission is instantaneous above threshold and absent below it**.

That is only explicable if a single photon of energy $h\nu$ must do the whole job in one go.

It is what won Einstein the Nobel Prize, and it is why light has to be granular.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum $p$ is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \mathbf{\dfrac{h}{p}}$.

Everything has one — a cricket ball's is about $10^{-34}$ m, which is why nobody has ever seen a ball diffract. For an electron it is comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electron diffraction works.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment depends on:
questions.solution:
$eV_{0} = h\nu - \phi$, so the stopping potential depends on the **frequency** and the metal's **work function** only.

Doubling the intensity doubles the current but leaves $V_{0}$ exactly where it was — the single most telling result of the whole experiment.
options: the frequency of light and the work function

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: The work function of a metal is:
questions.solution:
$\phi$ is the **minimum energy** to pull an electron out of the metal surface.

It fixes the threshold frequency, $\nu_{0} = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$ — the price of admission that every photon has to pay before anything is left over as kinetic energy.
options: the energy of the incident photon
the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface
the kinetic energy of the fastest electron
the energy of the metal's nucleus

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Find the threshold wavelength (in nm) for a metal of work function $2.48$ eV. Take $hc = 1240$ eV nm.
questions.solution:
$\lambda_{0} = \dfrac{hc}{\phi} = \dfrac{1240}{2.48} = \mathbf{500}$ nm.

Light of **longer** wavelength than this — redder, lower frequency — causes no emission at all.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Photons of energy $4$ eV fall on a metal of work function $1.5$ eV. Find the stopping potential, in volts.
questions.solution:
$eV_{0} = h\nu - \phi = 4 - 1.5 = 2.5$ eV, so $V_{0} = \mathbf{2.5}$ V.

Working in electron-volts makes the arithmetic trivial: the number of eV *is* the number of volts.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: de Broglie wavelength of an electron
questions.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength (in nm) of an electron accelerated through $150$ V, using $\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}$ nm.
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{150}} = \dfrac{1.227}{12.25} \approx \mathbf{0.1}$ nm.

That is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal — which is exactly why the Davisson–Germer experiment could diffract electrons off a nickel crystal and see the wave nature directly.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Find the energy (in eV) of a photon of wavelength $310$ nm. Take $hc = 1240$ eV nm.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: State Einstein's photoelectric equation and use it to explain the existence of a threshold frequency and the instantaneous nature of emission.
questions.solution:
**The equation.**

$h\nu = \phi + K_{\max}$, or $K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$.

A photon delivers all its energy $h\nu$ to **one** electron; $\phi$ is spent escaping the surface, the rest is kinetic energy.

**Threshold frequency.** $K_{\max}$ cannot be negative, so emission needs $h\nu \ge \phi$, that is $\nu \ge \nu_{0} = \dfrac{\phi}{h}$.

Below that frequency no photon, however many arrive, has enough energy — and intensity cannot help, because energy from two photons is not pooled.

**Instantaneous emission.** The whole transaction is one photon and one electron, so there is no waiting for energy to accumulate: emission begins within about $10^{-9}$ s.

Wave theory predicted a delay of minutes for faint light. None is observed. That is the experiment deciding between two theories.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: State the de Broglie hypothesis and derive the wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$.
questions.solution:
**The hypothesis.** Matter, like radiation, has a dual nature: a particle of momentum $p$ has an associated wavelength

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$.

**For an accelerated electron.** The work done by the field becomes kinetic energy:

$eV = \tfrac12 mv^{2} \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}$.

$p = mv = \sqrt{2meV}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$.

Putting the constants in gives the working form

$\mathbf{\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}}$, with $V$ in volts.

At $100$ V that is about $0.12$ nm — shorter than visible light by a factor of thousands, which is the whole reason the electron microscope can resolve what an optical one cannot.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Describe how the photoelectric effect is studied experimentally, and explain the three graphs: current against intensity, current against potential, and stopping potential against frequency.
questions.solution:
**Apparatus.** An evacuated tube with a photosensitive plate and a collector, a variable potential between them, a microammeter for the current, and monochromatic light of controllable frequency and intensity.

**Current against intensity** (frequency and potential fixed): a **straight line through the origin**. More photons per second means proportionally more electrons per second.

**Current against collector potential** (fixed frequency, two intensities): the current rises with potential and then **saturates** — every emitted electron is being collected. The saturation current is higher for greater intensity. Going negative, the current falls to zero at the **same** stopping potential for both intensities.

That last point is the crucial one: $V_{0}$ does not depend on intensity.

**Stopping potential against frequency:** a **straight line**,

$V_{0} = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$.

Its slope is $\dfrac{h}{e}$ — the **same for every metal**, which is how Millikan measured Planck's constant — and its intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold $\nu_{0}$, which differs from metal to metal.

Three graphs, one conclusion: light arrives in quanta.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Describe the Davisson-Germer experiment and say what it established.
questions.solution:
**Set-up.** Electrons from a heated filament are accelerated through a known potential and directed at a **nickel crystal**. A movable detector measures the intensity of electrons scattered at each angle.

**Observation.** The scattered intensity is not smooth: it shows a sharp **peak** at a particular angle (about $50°$ for $54$ V). Moving the detector round shows maxima and minima — a **diffraction pattern**.

**Interpretation.** The regular atomic planes of the crystal act as a diffraction grating. From Bragg's law the wavelength works out at about $0.165$ nm.

The de Broglie formula $\lambda = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{54}}$ nm predicts $0.167$ nm.

**What it established.** The agreement is the direct experimental proof that **electrons behave as waves** — matter waves are real, not a formal device.

Diffraction is a wave's signature. Particles are not supposed to do it. These did.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.q: Two metals have work functions $2$ eV and $4$ eV. Light of wavelength $310$ nm falls on both. Say which emits photoelectrons and find the maximum kinetic energy in that case.
questions.solution:
**Photon energy.** $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{310} = 4$ eV.

**Metal with $\phi = 2$ eV:** $4 > 2$, so emission occurs.

$K_{\max} = 4 - 2 = \mathbf{2}$ eV.

**Metal with $\phi = 4$ eV:** the photon energy exactly equals the work function, so an electron can just barely escape with **zero** kinetic energy. This is the threshold case — no photoelectric current worth measuring.

Doubling the intensity would not change either answer. Only a shorter wavelength would.
